entries.research_note: Goldman's retrospective explicitly describes confinement in a guarded cell. Forcade's interview dates the explosives acquittal to 1973. No jail register or original judgment was retrieved; dates and duration are omitted. Claims of a frame-up are not treated as judicial findings.

prisoner.name: Tom Forcade
prisoner.aka: Thomas King Forcade; Kenneth Gary Goodson
prisoner.description: Tom Forcade, also known as Thomas King Forcade and Kenneth Gary Goodson, oversaw the Underground Press Syndicate and founded High Times. Following the 1972 Miami political conventions, he faced a federal explosives prosecution. Albert Goldman's retrospective describes his confinement in a guarded jail cell; Forcade's later interview dates his acquittal to 1973. The surviving accounts reviewed do not establish exact custody dates or time served.

cases.charges: Federal explosives / firebomb-possession charge following the 1972 Miami conventions
cases.convicted: No — acquitted in 1973, according to his later interview
cases.sentence: Pretrial jail custody reported by Albert Goldman. Exact confinement dates and duration are unknown; the 1973 acquittal does not establish a release date.

entries.research_note: Bergman's recollection in the Reader explicitly confirms release on bail. The Reader says Calderon was cleared of all charges; Miller instead describes dismissal of syndicalism without a constitutional ruling and pleas by two unnamed co-defendants. Calderon's individual final disposition remains unresolved. Do not assign either plea or blanket exoneration to him.

prisoner.name: Carlos Calderon
prisoner.description: Carlos Calderon was a Brown Beret and an editor of El Barrio, a section of San Diego's Street Journal. He was one of Los Tres de San Diego prosecuted in 1970–71. A San Diego Reader history records actual confinement and release after newspaper colleagues raised bail. Accounts disagree about the prosecution's final outcome, so his individual disposition and exact custody duration remain unresolved.

cases.charges: Criminal syndicalism and solicitation of murder in the Los Tres de San Diego prosecution
cases.sentence: Held before release on bail in the 1970 prosecution. The Reader reports dismissal of all charges; defense organizer Arthur J. Miller describes pleas by two unnamed defendants on a remaining firebomb charge. Calderon's individual final disposition is unverified.

entries.research_note: The court and contemporary reporting connect Jerome/Jerry through the same OSU presidency and presidential-search committee. WOSU independently documents antiwar organizing. Newspaper employment is not established. The May 19 bail order is neither a release record nor the criminal case's disposition.

prisoner.name: Jerome Friedman
prisoner.description: Jerome 'Jerry' Friedman was Ohio State's undergraduate student president in 1971–72, an antiwar activist, and executive director of the Columbus Community Union. In May 1972 he was jailed under $100,000 bail. The reviewing court reduced it to $10,000, finding it unreasonable and discussing the original judge's objection to Friedman's criticism at a political meeting. His exact release date and final criminal disposition remain unverified.

cases.charges: Inciting to riot and disorderly conduct — Columbus, May 1972
cases.sentence: Pretrial detention under excessive bail; bond reduced May 19, 1972. No individual sentence, release date, or confinement duration has been verified.

entries.research_note: The court establishes custody; a signed memorial entry supplies Columbus antiwar context. Alternate spellings are duplicate-screening keys, not confirmation that every similarly named defendant is this person. No second case is inferred from the 1971 Detroit grand-jury lead or the earlier partly suspended Ravenna sentence.

prisoner.name: Colin Neiburger
prisoner.description: Colin Neiburger participated in the Columbus antiwar movement of the 1970s. A May 1972 court opinion documents his detention under $100,000 bail and reduces the bond to $10,000 as excessive. The opinion also discusses earlier violence-related matters; the bail ruling did not determine the pending charges. His exact confinement interval and final disposition remain unverified.

cases.charges: Inciting to riot and disorderly conduct — Columbus, May 1972
cases.sentence: Pretrial detention under excessive bail; bond reduced May 19, 1972. No individual sentence, release date, or confinement duration has been verified.

entries.research_note: The contemporary Door report establishes custody following conviction; OB Rag's editorial note gives May–December 1972. The Reader records Gormlie's recollection of about seven and one-half months. The defense account is attributed, and the successful appeal of newspaper-related probation restrictions is not described as reversal of the convictions. No day-level endpoints or numeric duration are inferred.

prisoner.name: Frank Gormlie
prisoner.description: Frank Gormlie founded the Ocean Beach People's Rag and organized in San Diego's Ocean Beach community. Following the 1971 Collier Park demonstration, he was convicted of failure to disperse and assault with a deadly weapon upon a police officer. His defense maintained that he used a shovel to protect a boy from police blows. OB Rag reports that he served from May to December 1972 and successfully appealed probation restrictions on association with the newspaper and its staff.

cases.charges: Failure to disperse from an unlawful assembly; assault with a deadly weapon upon a police officer — Collier Park demonstration
cases.sentence: Served May–December 1972; later recalled approximately seven and one-half months in jail. Newspaper-related probation restrictions were overturned on appeal. Exact custody endpoints and the sentence imposed remain unverified.

entries.research_note: Contemporary reporting establishes a resisting-arrest conviction arising from November 1970 garment-strike support, three days jailed during an appeal-stay lapse in 1972, and service of a six-month sentence on nights and weekends in 1973. Do not convert the intermittent sentence into six continuous months or add the three days without knowing custody credit. This entry covers the strike case; the separate May 1972 photography prosecution is not conflated with it.

prisoner.name: Ron Ridenour
prisoner.description: Ron Ridenour was a Los Angeles Free Press journalist and supporter of striking Chicana garment workers. He was arrested at a picket line in November 1970 and convicted of resisting arrest. The Militant reported in November 1973 that he was serving a six-month jail sentence on nights and weekends while allowed to work weekdays. The newspaper characterized the prosecution as a frame-up. This strike-support case was distinct from his later prosecution for photographing police at an antiwar protest.

cases.convicted: Yes — strike-support case; subsequent federal appeal outcome unverified
cases.sentence: Six-month jail sentence, reported being served on nights and weekends in November 1973, with weekday work permitted. A separate three-day confinement during an appeal-stay lapse was reported in 1972. Exact endpoints and total days actually confined are unknown.

entries.research_note: The Texas Observer's author note establishes an actual weekend in jail. The court opinion confirms the John D. Arnold name and dismissal of the contempt charges on January 9, 1974. The six-month sentence is not time served; the appellate decision is not a release date. Subsequent Sunday jail visits described in his article were reporting visits.

prisoner.name: J. D. Arnold
prisoner.description: J. D. Arnold, identified in court records as John D. Arnold, was news editor of the Dallas Iconoclast. The Texas Observer reported in July 1972 that he had recently spent a weekend in Dallas jail on contempt charges. The case arose from photographing an undercover officer outside a courtroom. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals dismissed the contempt charges on January 9, 1974; the six-month sentence imposed is not evidence of six months actually served.

cases.charges: Contempt of court — photographing an undercover officer outside a courtroom in April 1972
cases.convicted: Contempt adjudication; charges dismissed on appeal January 9, 1974
cases.sentence: Six months and a $500 fine imposed after a hearing; charges later dismissed. Actual custody documented: one weekend in 1972. Exact jail-entry and release dates are unknown.

entries.research_note: Abbott v. City of Columbus explicitly identifies the Columbus Free Press writer and states he was jailed in default of bail. The court reduced $20,000 bail to $3,000; conditional discharge does not show when he posted bond. Final disposition and duration are unknown. Do not merge this writer with the similarly named San Francisco poet.

prisoner.name: Steven Abbott
prisoner.description: Steven Abbott was a Columbus Free Press writer jailed in 1972 on riot-related misdemeanor charges. In Abbott v. City of Columbus, the reviewing court found no justification for his $20,000 bail and reduced it to $3,000. The state's adverse character evidence consisted of an article attributed to him, while the original bail decision had treated his charges as a felony. The opinion establishes actual detention but not its length or the final criminal outcome.

cases.charges: Second-degree riot, disorderly conduct, and malicious destruction of property — Columbus, 1972
cases.sentence: Pretrial detention under excessive bail. Bond reduced May 19, 1972 from $20,000 to $3,000. Exact release date, total confinement, and final criminal disposition are unverified.
